item.title: Psychology Is No Longer Alone
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Psychology Is No Longer Alone

Humans are never really alone. Neither is their psychology.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Every working hour now involves machines that shape what humans decide—the augmented hour is the default.
  • Machines trained on human text inherit human psychology and now show measurable Big Five variation.
  • Whether machines move from describing emotion to having it is undecided, perhaps undecidable from the outside.

By the time I sat down at my desk this morning, I had already relied on more machines than I can list cleanly. My phone had pushed me through three apps before I was upright. My watch said I slept well. The ring on my finger disagreed. A scheduling system had reorganized my morning around a conflict I had not yet seen. A drafting tool flagged two of last night's paragraphs as flat. Several language models were holding context I could no longer hold unaided: academic work, corporate writing, household logistics, wellness, and recovery. There is even a separate one for woodworking, because the vocabulary does not transfer. The night before, a streaming system chose the next episode, and I went to sleep later than I meant to.

I do not think of this as augmentation. I think of it as a normal morning. The augmented hour is the hour you are in.

Psychology has built itself around a particular subject: the human, studied as a bounded unit. What sits at most desks now is a human-plus-machine pair, performing tasks neither member could perform alone. The literature calls this distributed cognition—a tradition running from Edwin Hutchins's ship-navigation fieldwork to the Clark and Chalmers extended mind argument. Both were right early. The technology has now caught up.

A longer sociological argument goes further. From actor-network theory to recent entanglement work in educational technology, people and tools are not treated as separate units that later interact. They take shape together. The bounded individual was always a useful simplification. Social psychology has been socio-technical psychology longer than it has admitted.

The technology has also stepped out of screens. AI systems now operate in factories, clinics, warehouses, laboratories, classrooms, and phones. They do not merely answer questions. They shape attention, sequence tasks, filter options, and change what people notice before they decide.

In several narrow domains, machines now exceed the best humans. AlphaFold predicts protein structures at scales no laboratory can match, work recognized in the 2024 chemistry Nobel Prize. Stockfish has played chess at a superhuman level for two decades. Some medical-imaging tasks now match or exceed specialist performance. But the machine alone is not always the upper bound either. In well-designed pairings, expert humans working with strong AI can outperform either alone—a finding established in centaur chess and replicated in clinical decision-making since, especially when the task rewards intuition, context, or cross-domain transfer. The unit that performs is not the person or the machine. It is the pairing, designed well or badly—the operational reality I explored with Natan Linder in Augmented Lean.

Science fiction has long asked whether machines can feel: HAL, Data, Klara, Asimov's robots. The question still matters, but it is no longer the only one. Stevan Harnad called the strict objection the grounding problem: symbols defined only by other symbols never touch the ground. Whether machines move from describing emotion to having it is undecided, perhaps undecidable from the outside.

The grounding question still matters. But two other facts now matter to working psychology.

First, machines trained on human text inherit human psychology. They reproduce our biases, defaults, and emotional registers. They are statistical mirrors, and a mirror that flatters or amplifies can do damage at scale. Sherry Turkle has been documenting this trajectory for 40 years, from Alone Together through Reclaiming Conversation to the forthcoming Artificial Intimacy.

Second, machines now show measurable variation on instruments that psychology already uses. A 2025 Nature Machine Intelligence framework found that some large language models show Big Five personality patterns with surprising reliability, while comparative work found distinct profiles across ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok. These systems do not have stable inner dispositions. Their scores shift with both training and prompting. Training shapes baseline disposition; prompting shifts it at the surface. That instability does not make the finding useless. It makes the unit of analysis harder to ignore.

The unit of analysis has changed.

The diagnostic question I keep returning to is not about machines. It is about the discipline.

If your subjects spend most of their working hours coupled to systems that score on the same psychometric instruments your subjects do, what are you actually measuring when you measure them alone?

The honest answer is: a smaller part of them than psychology has assumed for most of its history. The work now is to study the rest.

item.title: Is There an Upside to Guilt?
item.description:
Guilt

Is There an Upside to Guilt?

Maybe it's not all that bad to feel guilty, or even ashamed, says new research.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Shame and guilt are unpleasant emotions that most people try to avoid, but might they have value?
  • A new study tests whether these emotions promote morality vs. harm your self-concept.
  • By considering the results of your actions and taking responsibility, you can become a more empathic person.

It’s impossible to go through life without doing something you regret. The uncomfortable feelings of guilt and shame often follow such mishaps. Jody felt terrible after blurting out a secret her partner told her in the presence of her partner’s family. Now, her partner refuses to speak to her, an understandable reaction. Jody is so overwhelmed with a combination of guilt and shame that she doesn’t know what to do. Maybe she should shove aside those feelings and move on, assuming (and hoping) that her partner will eventually forgive her.

The Adaptive Value of Guilt and Shame

According to a new study by Tsuinghua University’s Wenting Mu and colleagues (2026), some people are more prone to experience these feelings than others, reflecting enduring qualities that are the “affective core of important personality traits.” Furthermore, these reactions are “fundamental to moral functioning within social contexts” (p. 310). In other words, some people go from day to day constantly wondering what they've done wrong. This can make them miserable in the short term but better in the long term, as their sensitivity to harming others will bode well for the quality of their relationships.

One issue in deciding about the value of these trait-like propensities is deciding on how to distinguish between them. Shame comes from the realization that you’re a flawed human being and guilt from the awareness of flaws in your actions. A major problem in prior studies results from trying to separate these qualities through statistical methods before seeing how they relate to other aspects of personality (such as neuroticism or conscientiousness). Maybe they just are inextricably tied to each other, reflecting what Wu et al. believe to be a shared common factor.

In either case, the Tsuinghua U. researchers believe that you should not necessarily run away from these feelings when you’ve done something that produced ill effects. According to the Moral Emotion hypothesis, the tendency to feel shame and guilt promotes prosocial behaviors where you worry about the welfare of other people. From the perspective of the Self-Conscious Emotion hypothesis, though, the predilection to feel these emotions helps promote “self-awareness, self-reflection, and self-evaluation” (p. 311). Both of these hypotheses could be true; the purpose of the Mu et al. study was to test this out.

Testing Guilt, Shame, and Their Overlap

With the dual goals of finding out how much guilt and shame overlap as well as how they might promote moral and/or self-conscious behavior, the author team conducted three studies in which they tied guilt- and shame-proneness in relationship to other personality traits as well as the tendency to experience empathy, depression, anxiety, and narcissism.

To give you an idea of how the authors measured guilt and shame, here are some sample items:

Guilt:

You make plans to meet a friend for lunch. At 5 o’clock, you realize you stood him up. You think you should make it up to him as soon as possible.

You attend your co-worker’s housewarming party and you spill red wine on their new cream-colored carpet but you think no one notices. You would stay late to help clean up the stain after the party.

Shame:

For several days you put off making a difficult phone call. At the last minute, you make the call and are able to manipulate the conversation so that all goes well. You would feel like a coward.

You are out with friends one evening and you’re feeling especially witty and attractive. Your best friend’s spouse seems to particularly enjoy your company. You would think: “I should have been aware of what my best friend is feeling.”

Using a combination of online adult and undergraduate samples, Mu et al. found that, as they predicted, guilt and shame shared considerable overlap. This general factor, in turn, allowed the authors to find evidence in support of the Moral Emotion hypothesis, revealing that people high on these traits are also high on the qualities of empathy, as well as the personality traits of agreeableness and conscientiousness. These combinations, in turn, appeared to be protective in terms of what’s called “externalizing psychopathology,” or the tendency to harm others (e.g. through grandiose narcissism).

There was only mixed support for the self-conscious emotion hypothesis, as high scores on shame and guilt were not related to feelings of self-consciousness or internalizing psychopathology (e.g., vulnerable narcissism).

The findings clearly support, then, the value of experiencing shame, guilt, and the combination of the two when you’ve transgressed against others. Also consistent with the theoretical model, shame appeared to be more inwardly focused (what’s wrong with me?) and guilt toward a desire to repair the hurt you’ve created (how can I fix this?).

Using Guilt and Shame to Your Advantage

You might argue that being too hard on yourself after you’ve done something that hurts someone else can become counterproductive in terms of adaptation. If we think of Jody as being inconsolable after violating her partner’s trust, it might seem that she should be able to reach a point of being able to go on with her life and their relationship.

However, from the moral emotion standpoint, maybe she shouldn’t. Showing her partner how sorry she is and even, yes, feeling that she failed, would allow her to use the experience to deepen both their relationship and her own self-understanding. Maybe she does tend to overshare and needs to ask herself why. Perhaps realizing how much she hurt her partner could also help her come to a deeper realization of how much her partner means to her. Sharing her reaction with her partner could help both of them repair the damage and the toll this all took on their relationship.

To sum up, you may think that getting rid of guilt and not feeling ashamed is an adaptive way to handle your failures. As the Mu et al. study shows, this will not prove, in the long run, to help you develop and deepen your ability to have fulfillment either in your own self-understanding or your relationships.

item.title: What Psychotherapists Need to Know to Treat Family Caregivers
item.description:
Caregiving

What Psychotherapists Need to Know to Treat Family Caregivers

Traditionally trained psychotherapists can use their skills to support caregivers.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Psychotherapists need to be prepared to work with clients who are family caregivers.
  • Psychoeducation is crucial when working with caregiver clients.
  • Focused psychotherapeutic approaches are called for with caregiver clients.

When a 45-year-old woman called seeking an appointment for treatment of depression and anxiety, the psychotherapist assumed she would be a standard case. But during the initial visit, the client said her symptoms had a specific cause: Caring for her father with dementia and two teenage daughters while also holding down a full-time job was stressing her out. Her story gave the therapist pause. Would typical psychotherapeutic modalities help this client? Or would she need a specialized treatment focused on managing caregiving’s many challenges?

As our country ages and the number of American family caregivers continues to rise—from 43.5 million in 2014 to 63 million in 2024, according to the 2025 Caregiving in the U.S. report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving—more psychotherapists are fielding calls from prospective clients in the midst of caregiving. To provide care that is appropriate, competent, and effective, those therapists usually realize that they need at least some understanding of caregiving stress. They aren’t sure, however, what ideal caregiver therapy looks like.

Although no professional organization has yet developed formal clinical guidelines in this area, decades of research on caregiver needs and potential interventions point to some general competencies for helping caregivers. As psychologists specializing in caregiver therapy for more than 30 years, we offer these key points that we make to therapists who would like to work with this population:

Psychoeducation

It is not uncommon for family caregivers like the daughter mentioned above to feel lost and overwhelmed in their caregiving journeys by the sheer amount of essential information and skills they need to master on medical procedures, managing finances and insurance paperwork, and coordinating multiple support services. Therapists should be able to provide basic guidance for navigating this confusing landscape, including psychoeducation on:

  • Normal emotional reactions to being a caregiver, ranging from sadness to anger to guilt, as well as the potential negative impacts (increased stress, depression, and anxiety) and positive rewards (personal and spiritual growth, the opportunity to give back) of being a caregiver. This should also include expectable reactions—often relief, followed by guilt about having felt relieved, followed by sadness—to the care receiver’s death and the end of caregiving.
  • Ideas for self-care, including time management techniques, respite, mindfulness practices, and limit-setting. Therapists can also give permission to caregivers who feel guilty about needing to take time to care for themselves.
  • Care receivers’ medical conditions—such as dementia, Parkinson’s disease, heart failure, COPD, and cancer—the typical course and prognosis for that condition, and its usual treatments, treatment efficacy, and side effects.
  • Navigating our complex, fragmented health systems to find the right providers and services for care receivers. This includes learning how to communicate with busy doctors to develop working partnerships with them.

Psychotherapeutic Approaches

For caregivers in acute distress, psychoeducation alone is necessary but not sufficient. In these cases, there are several types of psychotherapy that are helpful if used with adaptations and for specific purposes:

  • Insight-oriented therapy: The relationship between a caregiver and care receiver can be fraught because of their pre-caregiving history. For example, if an older adult was a neglectful or abusive parent, an adult child caregiver may feel more conflicted and therefore more stressed about caring for them. By helping caregivers gain insight into those early relationships and how they are coloring their emotional reactions to the caregiving situation, therapists can help caregivers better separate past issues from current challenges to focus more readily on meeting the present needs of a now frail and vulnerable parent.
  • Cognitive behavioral therapy: Under this broad category, there are several psychotherapies that can be useful for caregivers. Traditional cognitive behavioral therapy, which strives to correct irrational thoughts, can be applied to the perfectionistic tendencies of caregivers whose expectations for the care they should provide are set too high and who then experience unrealistic guilty feelings for “failing.” Problem-solving therapy can be used to teach caregivers a process for thinking through the inevitable problems that arise during caregiving, generating solutions, and then choosing and implementing the most promising one. Assertiveness training can encourage caregivers to set limits with care receivers who make too many demands or solicit assistance from family members who are contributing too little to the caregiving effort. Acceptance and commitment therapy, with its emphasis on clarifying personal values, can strengthen caregivers’ motivation for and commitment to providing care for a family member
  • Family systems therapy: It is family conflict between adult siblings or a well and ill spouse that often leads frustrated and angry caregivers to seek psychotherapy. Family therapy techniques, including couples and family sessions, can reduce that conflict, create greater family cohesion and cooperation, and thereby decrease caregiving stress
  • Grief therapy: Caregivers suffer many losses during caregiving. Because of the sacrifices of time and energy they make, they grieve their previous routine and, often, sense of personal freedom. They grieve the slow loss of their care receiver to a progressive condition such as dementia or Parkinson’s disease. Eventually, they grieve that family member’s death. Naming that grief in its different forms, including anticipatory grief and ambiguous loss, is often helpful for validating caregivers’ experiences and emotions. Other grief therapy techniques—for instance, recalling cherished memories, creating tender interactions with the care receiver to cherish later, and employing grief rituals—can help them better contain their sadness and make positive meanings of their months and years of caregiving.

The take-home point here is that there are many ways that traditionally trained psychotherapists can expand their knowledge and flex their skills to support caregivers. The work, focused on high-stakes life and death issues, can be highly emotional for the caregiver and therapist. In our experience, it is also deeply gratifying.

item.title: The Magnetic Sense
item.description:
Animal Behavior

The Magnetic Sense

Why do dogs defecate from north to south? It's about the Earth's magnetic field.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Many species are sensitive to the Earth's magnetic field.
  • Many species use the Earth’s magnetic field lines to navigate.
  • Many species also align themselves with the Earth's magnetic field, but it is unclear why.
  • Humans might also possess a magnetic sense, but it is subconscious.

It was one of the most widely mocked studies in the field of animal cognition. A team from Germany and the Czech Republic found that dogs prefer to defecate with their bodies aligned along the Earth's magnetic field (Hart et al. 2013). Really? Do scientists really have nothing better to do than study how dogs poop?

Of course, there is much more to it than that. This study shows that dogs have a special skill: They are sensitive to the Earth's magnetic field. It is now known that other species, including birds, sea turtles, reptiles, insects, bacteria, and plants, also use the geomagnetic field. Humans may also have a magnetic sense, but it is subconscious (Chae et al., 2022). Our brains may sense the magnetic field, but we are not aware of it. As I wrote here previously, it is very challenging to study skills in which animals outperform us. In this case, we scientists must try to imagine what it is like to possess a sense that we lack.

Orientation in space

What do we know about the magnetic sense in the animal kingdom? The proper definition for the magnetic sense is “the ability of organisms to detect the Earth's magnetic field”. Why was that skill developed during evolution, and what are the obvious benefits for magnetosensitive animals? They can use their special sense for orientation and spatial navigation. The advantage of the Earth's magnetic field is that it is everywhere. When we use vision, we need light, and when we use sound, there are also obvious limits, e.g., sounds do not travel very far. And magnetic cues are also available in deep oceans, underground, or at night (Lam & Malkemper, 2026).

Many species use the polarity or inclination of the Earth’s magnetic field lines to navigate, meaning they rely on a magnetic compass. The European robin was the first species to become famous for this. This is a bird that migrates at night. In a remarkable experiment conducted in the 1970s, these birds were placed in a funnel-shaped test cage during the migratory season. They attempted to escape. The poor birds left scratch marks on the walls of the funnel. It transpired that these marks were northward in spring and southward in autumn, corresponding with the direction of their migration. Therefore, the magnetic field lines guided the robins' behaviour (Wiltschko & Wiltschko, 1972). Many other bird species, as well as fish, amphibians, insects and mice, have been shown to use the magnetic compass. Further studies have found that many of these species determine their position using landmarks, for example, and then choose a suitable compass orientation to navigate to their destination. This is called 'true navigation' (Lam & Malkemper, 2026).

Alignment

In addition to orientation in space, the phenomenon of alignment also occurs, as mentioned above. This refers to the way in which animals align themselves with the Earth's magnetic field. It is not only dogs that do that. Red foxes, for example, align with the Earth's magnetic field when they hunt mice. They jump high to surprise their prey from above. Foxes often jump towards the northeast, and attacks from this direction are especially successful (Červený et al. 2011). Cattle are also often seen in alignment with the Earth's magnetic field, as are insects, reptiles, fish, birds, deer and wild boar. But why? To be honest, we are not exactly sure. Some speculate that it may be related to the coordination of herding behaviour, the calibration of the magnetic compass or simply because it 'feels better'. These explanations are not very convincing, are they? They do not really answer the question of why dogs poo aligned from north to south, or vice versa. However, I am optimistic that scientists are "smarter than you think". At some point they will find a way to figure it out.

item.title: When Eating Less Feels Like Caring Less
item.description:
Appetite

When Eating Less Feels Like Caring Less

The unexpected relational challenges facing millions of GLP-1 users.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Food is an important form of social currency that facilitates relationships.
  • The social currency of food declines in value among GLP-1 medicine users.
  • The loss of food as social currency can create many types of relationship challenges.

Rosa and her friend Cheryl had lunch together on the first Saturday of every month for 21 years. They had walked adjacent routes through the same San Diego neighborhoods for most of their postal service careers, retired within months of each other, and built those Saturday lunches into something that outlasted careers and even their children's school years. They always went to the same Mexican restaurant. Rosa always ordered the same thing.

Until, suddenly, she didn't.

Weeks after starting a GLP-1 medicine, Rosa's appetite changed. The portions felt too large. Her usual anticipatory excitement for the meal waned. She began ordering soup and a small appetizer, even then leaving most of it behind. Within a few months, Cheryl started canceling their lunches; never abruptly, always with plausible reasons.

Rosa didn't think Cheryl was angry. But she realized that the GLP-1 treatment had taken something special away that was hard to put into words.

It wasn't the food. It was the social language that food had been speaking to them for two decades.

Food Is Never Just Food

Most of us appreciate that food carries social meaning. What we underestimate, until disrupted, is how much of our relational infrastructure food subtly holds together.

Food has long served as a primary currency for human connection.1 We mark every significant life transition with eating: births, weddings, funerals, promotions, reunions. We express love through cooking and receive it through eating. We build friendships over shared meals. Presidents and CEOs seal negotiations over business dinners. The "Last Supper" painting is an immortalized work of art. The phrase "breaking bread" is thousands of years old, yet its resonance hasn't faded because the function it describes hasn't either.

At the individual level, food serves as stress relief, reward, comfort, and entertainment. At the relational level, it is an act of care. At the cultural level, food organizes our collective rituals so thoroughly that we rarely notice until the pattern breaks. Thanksgiving. The Super Bowl spread. The office birthday. The wedding dinner. These aren't events that happen to involve food. Food is a central part of what makes these events memorable human experiences.

This layered reality, food as individual comfort, social currency, and cultural ritual, runs so deep that it largely operates beneath conscious awareness. Which is precisely why it becomes so disruptive when it suddenly changes.

The GLP-1 Difference

People have always felt social consequences when they changed their eating habits. Someone going vegan or cutting carbs temporarily disrupts social eating, for example. But those changes are generally understood as choices, and they come with a convenient explanation the people around them can process: "I'm trying something new," or "I can't eat that right now."

The GLP-1 experience is categorically different.

GLP-1 medicines work by restoring hormonal signaling in the brain's appetite and reward systems. The result is a neurobiological change: an often profound reduction in the motivational pull of food that is likely to persist as long as the medicine continues. Users commonly describe not just eating less, but caring less about food. They've become someone for whom the social, emotional, and sensory reward of food is substantially reduced. Not by personal preference but by biological rewiring.

And because the change continues while a person takes these medications, its social ripple effects don't resolve after a few awkward dinners. They require active navigation.

Navigating the New Landscape

Understanding that this transition is biological, not volitional, is the navigational foundation for the GLP-1 user and the people in their lives. A few practical strategies arise from this foundation.

  1. Label the change, starting with yourself. Many GLP-1 users feel guilty about their changed relationship with food, often without being able to articulate why. Naming it directly, such as "Food meant more to me and to the people around me than I realized, and that's changing," converts a diffuse social discomfort into something tangible that can be addressed. Rosa's insight that her treatment had taken something away from the friendship was painful but useful. It gave her something to work with.
  2. Separate your appetite from your affection, and communicate it to others. For people whose love language is food, eating less can register as caring less.2 This misread is almost inevitable unless it's preempted. A direct and warm statement goes a long way: "The food is wonderful, and so is the fact that you made it. My appetite is just much smaller now." Specificity matters here. Vague reassurance is less effective than speaking the dynamic clearly. And, usually, more than once.
  3. Propose new rituals rather than mourning old ones. If Saturday lunch was really about celebrating Rosa and Cheryl's friendship, then the meal was never essential. But someone has to say that, and someone has to propose something to replace the old ritual. A walk. Coffee. A different kind of gathering that the friendship can live inside without food as its primary structure. Friendships that survive this transition tend to do so because someone explicitly invested in finding a new opportunity.
  4. Help the people around you understand the biology. Avoid lectures. But a brief explanation of what GLP-1 medicines actually do can reframe a lot of confusion and hurt feelings. Most people's mental model is that GLP-1 users are "on a diet." Knowing that the change is physical, not personal, can shift the relational dynamic from complication to curiosity. People usually extend more openness to a biology they understand than to a choice they're taking as personal offense.
  5. Expect some grief on both sides, and give it room. Some of what GLP-1 users and their social networks are navigating is a sense of loss: a shared language, a familiar ritual, a way of being together that organized their relationships for years. That loss doesn't cancel the benefits of the medicine. But it is meaningful, and treating it as such, rather than expecting the transition to be purely celebratory, enables more honest discussion and opportunities for change.

---------------

Rosa and Cheryl eventually had the conversation they'd been avoiding. It took a few months and a direct question from Rosa: I miss our Saturdays. Do you? What followed was a candid hour—about their friendship, about what those lunches had meant, about what Cheryl was feeling that she hadn't known how to say. They still have lunch on the first Saturday of every month. Rosa still orders the soup. Cheryl has stopped tracking what's on her plate. Their friendship was always about more than food. They just needed the food to change to see that clearly.

item.title: Post-Traumatic Solutions
item.description:
Resilience

Post-Traumatic Solutions

The meaning we ascribe to an experience may matter more than the experience itself.

Posted June 9, 2026

Resilience
Source: Michele Weiner-Davis/ Used with Permission

Last week I did an intensive and worked with a young woman whose life was transformed by a story I shared with her.

Although discussing childhood experiences is not the focus of my work with couples during intensives, Sharon talked a great deal about how she was raised. To say that she had it tough would be a vast understatement. Both of her parents were drug addicts and unable to properly nurture or protect their 6 children. As is often the case in chaotic families, the children “raised each other.”

Sharon shared that her parents divorced when she was 6, and that although her mother was working on becoming sober, her father was a heroin addict. Still, she was sent to her dad’s house for regular visits.

Her father often had other drug addicts hanging around his house when she visited. One of these men, Sharon said, sexually abused her. This happened on several occasions. Additionally, Sharon admitted that her own brother sexually abused her for 4 years and told her that he would hurt her if she ever told anyone. She never did.

As Sharon talked about these experiences, she cried, explaining that she felt shame and disgust because she allowed these things to happen in her life. Even though the abuse had happened long ago, the feeling of self-contempt was omnipresent. She believed that, somehow, she should have stopped the abuse.

I reminded Sharon that she was just a little girl when the abuse took place and that it was not her fault; her parents should have protected her. A wonderful protective parent today of three young children, she agreed, but still, she had been unable to shake the feeling that she was damaged goods.

That’s when I knew I had to tell her a story of a client whom I worked with many years before.

This client told me that she lived alone and that she was runner; every day at the same time, she would set off on her run, taking the same path.

One day, she returned to her apartment after her run, and the door closed behind her. There stood a masked man with a knife in his hand. At once, she realized that she might get raped, but was determined that she would get out of the situation alive. The man did, in fact, rape her, but when he got distracted for a moment, she got out of his grip, and ran across the street to a neighbor’s house stark naked.

The neighbor gave her some clothes and called the police. The police arrived and interrogated her as to what had just happened. This woman calmly and carefully outlined the events that had taken place.

Noting her calm demeanor, the policeman said, “Ma'am, I don’t get it. You were just raped at knifepoint and you are telling me this story so calmly. How is that possible?”

Her response forever changed my thinking about traumatic experiences. Here’s what she told the cop: “You don’t think that I’m going to let 15 minutes with that f---er ruin my life, do you?”

The rape did not ruin her life. For years, she volunteered at a rape crisis center, supporting other victims. She took pride in her resilience and wanted to share her perspective with others.

I watched Sharon’s face when I told her this story. Her eyes lit up. She smiled. Her body relaxed. I hoped that this story of resilience would begin to percolate in Sharon’s mind.

The next day, Sharon began the session by saying that a gigantic weight had been lifted. She said that all of her life, she had felt dirty and unworthy. But after hearing that story, she felt relief. Sharon told me that she looked in the mirror that morning, and for the first time, she liked what she saw.

Perhaps as you read this story and how my client of so long ago responded to that vile act that day, you might have been thinking, “Was she in denial?” “Won’t she eventually experience PTSD if she doesn’t do a deep dive into the trauma of what happened?” “Don’t victims of sexual crimes require years of therapy to heal their spirits?”

I get it. There was a time in my career that I would have thought those things too.

But after decades of working with people, I’ve learned that everyone is different, and how we deal with life experiences differs greatly.

How ludicrous it is to believe that each person must go through the same process to heal. How wonderful it is to know that the meaning we ascribe to our experiences is even more significant than the experiences themselves.

As this young couple left the intensive, the woman gave me a hug that nearly took my breath away because she squeezed me so hard. I had to fight back tears because I understood the emotion behind her embrace.

item.title: The Empirical Record on Conflict at Work
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

The Empirical Record on Conflict at Work

What you always wanted to know about conflict in the workplace but didn't ask.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Most workplace conflict correlates with lower performance and satisfaction, not higher.
  • Cooperative goals and interdependence, not raw friction, fuel real team problem-solving.
  • Personality traits have little impact; team structure and norms matter far more.
A Diagram of Published Research on Good Conflict
Source: ChatGPT Generated

For a generation, leaders have been sold a seductive story about disagreement: that great teams fight, that friction breeds genius, that if your meetings are too polite, something is quietly rotting. We've turned conflict into a virtue signal. "Disagree and commit." "Strong opinions, loosely held." "If two people always agree, one of them is unnecessary." It sounds bracingly honest. It is also, according to actual science, mostly wrong.

The empirical record on constructive conflict resolution—through organizational psychology, negotiation research, and decades of family studies—delivers a finding that should unsettle every leader who has ever congratulated themselves on running a "candid" room. Task disagreement, on its own, does not reliably make teams better. Meta-analytic research perpetually finds that both relationship conflict and task conflict often correlate negatively with performance and satisfaction. Conflict pays off only under narrow, fragile conditions: When it stays moderate, stays about ideas, and never curdles into a contest over status, loyalty, or worth. The romantic image of productive friction is the exception, not the rule. And most workplaces manufacture the rule.

If more arguing isn't the answer, what is?

The science is refreshingly specific. The single strongest predictor of whether disagreement becomes generative, much to my mentor Morton Deutsch’s delight, is cooperative goals; structuring the work so that people genuinely need one another's success. Dean Tjosvold and colleagues have shown across cultures and industries that mutual-benefit interdependence changes the very meaning of a disagreement: it stops being a duel to win and becomes a problem to solve together. Stack on psychological safety, norms, and leadership that legitimize dissent, and the belief that the team can survive a hard conversation, and you get the real engine: open-minded discussion, perspective-taking, joint problem-solving. That combo, not raw conflict, is what produces better decisions, faster learning, higher performance, and more durable relationships.

What is conspicuously absent from the top of that list? Personality. Demographics. The charismatic truth-teller who "isn't afraid to say what everyone's thinking." A Big Five meta-analysis confirms that traits matter only at the margins; neuroticism nudges people toward avoidance, agreeableness toward compromise, but they are dwarfed by factors leaders can actually change. This is the provocation buried in the data: we have been treating conflict as a character issue when it is overwhelmingly a design issue. We recruit for "tough-minded" people and hold "courageous conversations" workshops, when the highest-leverage move is to redraw incentives, rewrite norms, and rebuild the structure of the conversation itself (by the way, the same is true for highly peaceful societies).

The leadership implications are blunt, and they indict much current practice.

First, stop celebrating heat and start engineering safety and security. The leader who prizes blunt clashes without first establishing that no one will be punished for them isn't building candor; they're building a coliseum, where the powerful perform boldness and everyone else learns to go quiet. Negotiation research is unambiguous here too: power asymmetry corrodes integrative outcomes, because the powerful threaten more, listen less, and take others' perspectives least. If you are the most senior person in the room, your appetite for "robust debate" is not evidence of a healthy culture. It may be the very thing suppressing it.

Second, defend the boundary between the idea and the person with your life. Constructive conflict lives or dies on keeping disagreement about the work from becoming disagreement about the worth of the people doing it. The moment a critique of an argument is heard as a verdict on a colleague's competence, loyalty, or place in the tribe, you have crossed from the generative loop into the destructive one: this is the escalation spiral that family research has documented for decades, where demands meet withdrawal, and the relationship erodes.

Third, respect the cognitive cost. Genuine problem-solving: listening, reframing, generating options, and integrating opposing views, is metabolically expensive. Rushed, fatigued, deadline-strangled teams don't rise to the occasion; they collapse into positional bargaining and rigid certainty. If your "we move fast and challenge each other" culture runs on chronic time pressure, you have optimized for the conditions under which constructive conflict is least possible.

The deeper reframe is this. Good conflict is not a personality you hire, a brave moment you summon, or a slogan you stencil on the wall. It is an environment you build and rebuild, deliberately, against the natural drift of every group toward either false harmony or open warfare. The leaders who understand this will stop asking "how do I get my people to speak up?" and start asking "what about this room makes speaking up so costly?"

That question is harder. It points back at the leader rather than the team. Which is precisely why so few are willing to ask it — and why those who do will outthink, outlearn, and outlast the rest.
